statement: On April 29, 2026, in Louisiana v. Callais the Supreme Court held that Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is violated only when the evidence supports a strong inference that a state intentionally drew districts to give minority voters less opportunity because of their race.
anchor: On April 29, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court in Louisiana v. Callais significantly narrowed the circumstances under which a racial vote dilution challenge to a redistricting map can be made under Section 2
only when the evidence supports a strong inference that the State intentionally drew its districts to afford minority voters less opportunity because of their race
context: CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11431, 2026-05-14 (nonpartisan summary of a court holding; the opinion is primary law, vote 6-3 per the Brennan Center page). Holding stands in January 2029 unless Congress amends Section 2 or the Court revisits it; CRS lists race-neutral amendments or codifying the modified Gingles framework as options.

statement: CRS expects Callais to change how maps are drawn: existing majority-minority districts drawn to comply with Section 2 may be challenged as racial gerrymanders, and some legislatures were already modifying maps for the 2026 elections.
anchor: Existing majority-minority districts that were designed to comport with Section 2 might be challenged as unconstitutional racial gerrymanders in view of Callais
some state legislatures are considering or have already enacted modifications to their redistricting maps that eliminate majority-minority districts for the upcoming 2026 congressional elections
context: CRS, 2026-05-14. The sidebar's dissent summary (Justice Kagan) says plaintiffs must now prove a race-based motive, 'nearly impossible'; the majority says the update reflects social change since 1986. Contested: the Brennan Center says the ruling will make Section 2 cases 'much harder' to win; the Manhattan Institute argued before the decision that the problem lay in the Gingles framework, not the statute.

statement: The Brennan Center says Callais made three changes to the Gingles framework that together will make it much harder for voters of color to win Section 2 cases.
anchor: collectively will make it much harder for voters of color to win cases filed under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act
context: Brennan Center (left-leaning), updated after the decision. Agrees with CRS on direction; goes further on effect. The Brennan page also notes nearly half of all Section 2 cases since 1982 challenged at-large local elections, so local effects may be larger than the congressional-map focus suggests (not independently checked).
locator: Brennan Center page, text beginning 'On April 29, 2026'

statement: The Manhattan Institute argued, before the decision, that the problem in Callais lay with the Gingles framework rather than with the Voting Rights Act, which expressly disavows proportional representation.
anchor: The problem lies not with the statute but with Thornburg v. Gingles
context: Manhattan Institute (right-leaning), written 2025-10-24 before the ruling; included as the contesting view. It says the 1982 amendment disavows any right to proportional representation. The majority in Callais adopted a similar reading of Gingles.

statement: The Supreme Court's 2013 decision in Shelby County v. Holder invalidated the Voting Rights Act coverage formula, which rendered preclearance inoperable, while the nationwide Section 2 ban on race-based voting rules remains.

Section 2 of the act contains a nationwide prohibition on voting qualifications based on race, color, or language-minority status.
context: CRS R47520, updated 2026-06-03. The formula relied on 1960s and 1970s turnout data and covered mostly Southern states; a new formula would need present-day justification (CRS). Preclearance returns only if Congress enacts a new formula or a court orders 'bail-in'; no such law is enacted as of this report.

statement: On June 30, 2026, in NRSC v. FEC the Supreme Court invalidated the federal statutory limits on coordinated party expenditures.
anchor: On June 30, 2026, in National Republican Senatorial Committee v. Federal Election Commission ( NRSC v. FEC ), the U.S. Supreme Court invalidated federal statutory limits on a type of political party spending known as coordinated party expenditures .
context: CRS IF13270, 2026-07-16. The vote was 6-3 with Justice Kavanaugh writing and Colorado II overruled, per a law-firm alert (Covington, 2026-06) and Al Jazeera; the CRS In Focus gives background only and says legal analysis is beyond its scope. The limits had been set by a formula; for 2026 the House limit in a single-district state was $130,600 and the 2024 presidential limit was about $32.4 million. The Court left party-to-candidate contribution limits ($5,000 per candidate, per election) in place.

statement: CRS says the effects of NRSC v. FEC are still in flux: unlimited coordinated party spending could help parties compete with super PACs, or could raise corruption risks in party fundraising, and the practical effect may be larger in the 2028 cycle and beyond.
anchor: Some observers have argued that unlimited coordinated expenditures could help parties compete with the financial influence of super PACs or other entities making IEs. Others counter that unlimited coordinated expenditures could increase corruption risks in party fundraising.
it is possible that practical implications from the ruling could be more substantial in the 2028 election cycle and beyond.
context: CRS, 2026-07-16, presents both views without choosing. Covington (practitioner view) says party committees will become a much more attractive vehicle for campaign financing; Senate Democrats quoted by Al Jazeera call the decision an invitation for corruption.

statement: Herd and Moynihan argue that administrative burdens, meaning learning, compliance and psychological costs, reduce program take-up and fall hardest on the disadvantaged.

The counter-position is that verification and documentation requirements protect program integrity (see improper payment rates in E-G33), which these studies do not measure; E-G38 also shows reducing frictions can reach less needy people.
